records.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how demography and natural selection interact during colonization of novel environments is a central question in evolutionary biology. The Baltic Sea region combines one of the world's strongest salinity gradients with a well‐characterized postglacial history of less than ~12,000 years. The harbour porpoise ( Phocoena phocoena ) is distributed across this gradient as three populations—the North Sea, Belt Sea and Proper Baltic Sea populations. Using whole genome resequencing data from 59 individuals, we reconstructed the demographic history of Baltic colonization and identified genomic signatures of local adaptation. Demographic modelling supported a sequential colonization in which the Belt Sea population diverged first from an ancestral North Sea population, followed by an independent divergence of the Proper Baltic Sea population, with two equally supported timing hypotheses placing initial colonization either during the Yoldia Sea (~11,800 years ago) or the Baltic Sea period (~8000 years ago). The Proper Baltic Sea population showed drift‐dominated divergence consistent with a founder effect, while two discrete genomic islands of differentiation with selective sweep signatures were identified between North and Belt Sea populations, pointing to recent positive selection. Both regions contain osmoregulatory candidate genes, most notably SCNN1D, encoding part of the epithelial Na + channels, a key regulator of sodium homeostasis. A non‐synonymous mutation in SCNN1D showed striking allele frequency divergence along the salinity gradient, confirmed across ~400 individuals. Together, these results reveal how genetic drift and divergent selection interact to drive rapid adaptation to a brackish environment, and identify SCNN1D as a compelling candidate for cetacean osmoregulatory adaptation.
records.title: Drift and Selection in a Recently Colonized Sea: The Genomic Basis of Adaptation to Low‐Salinity Waters in Baltic Harbour Porpoises

records.abstract: The conservation of lesser-known and data-deficient species poses significant challenges globally, particularly in developing countries such as Nepal, which harbor rich biodiversity but face resource constraints that affect scientific capacity. Furthermore, young researchers from countries such as Nepal often encounter numerous hurdles when deciding whether to pursue wildlife research or shift to other career paths. In this paper, we present a methodological approach to studying data-deficient and lesser-known species, a step-by-step roadmap that guides aspiring conservationists from step zero (the very beginning) to successfully securing sufficient funds and implementing long-lasting, impactful projects. The framework is based on a practice-oriented, experiential, and applied conservation research framework in wildlife conservation in Nepal. This framework encompasses critical steps such as species assessment, literature review, training, research planning, resource acquisition, outreach, community engagement, and conservation action planning. Case studies on the fishing cat, Eurasian otter, and owl species illustrate the practical application of these steps, highlighting successful strategies and lessons learned. The paper emphasizes the importance of collaboration, capacity building, and innovative approaches such as social media engagement and incentive-based conservation. Drawing on real-world experiences, it offers valuable insights and guidance for aspiring conservationists, providing a roadmap for navigating the complexities of wildlife conservation in resource-limited yet biodiversity-rich regions.
records.title: A practice-based approach for conservation of lesser-known species: a lesson learned from the last decade in Nepal

records.abstract: ABSTRACT Assessing foraging behavior of harbor porpoise ( Phocoena phocoena ) from acoustic data has become increasingly common. Yet, a wide range of analytical methods is currently used, often without formal evaluation of their comparability. This lack of cross‐method validation limits the ability to compare findings across studies and interpret differences in reported foraging activity. This study addressed this challenge by providing a systematic comparative evaluation of acoustic foraging detection methods, while introducing a novel refinement, the Search Buzz Foraging Identification (SBFI) method. We aimed to quantify the degree of similarity of the SBFI method alongside four established methods that use acoustic data and more specifically inter‐click intervals to identify foraging behavior. All methodologies were applied to the same F‐POD dataset collected at two locations for a full year. Comparability among methods was evaluated using correlation, distance, and trend analyses to assess agreement in relative patterns, absolute magnitude, and temporal dynamics. Most methods indicated strong agreement in relative foraging patterns and temporal trends; however, differences in magnitude and context‐dependent biases emerged under specific spatial or seasonal conditions, suggesting methods are not completely interchangeable. The SBFI method showed strong correlation with several existing methods while providing a comprehensive and accessible framework for identifying foraging behavior. This study gives a systemic overview of existing foraging metrics and provides a basis for improved comparability and interpretation of acoustic‐based foraging studies.
records.title: A Novel Method to Infer Harbor Porpoise Foraging Behavior From Acoustic Data: A Comparative Assessment Against Established Techniques

records.abstract: Vocal production learning is a rare skill that requires neural control over the sound production system. This control is often either laryngeal (phonatory) or supralaryngeal; in a few species, such as humans, it involves both. Recent neurobiological evidence suggests that phocine seals possess neural wiring similar to humans for laryngeal vocal learning. Within this branch, grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) can modify sounds through supralaryngeal control, but can they also control vocalizations through the larynx itself? To test this, we trained an adult male with positive reinforcement to increase the fundamental frequency (f 0) within a single vocalization, i.e. adjust its Δf 0. Using a custom-made semi-automatic setup that enabled f 0 live-tracking, we show that the seal expanded his Δf 0 from a pre-experimental median of 22.6 Hz to a median of 345 Hz in the final session, thereby demonstrating remarkable phonatory control. Our results complement behavioural evidence in other pinnipeds, showing that phocines exhibit not only respiratory and supralaryngeal control but also, as we show here, fine laryngeal control. These findings align with independent neurobiological evidence, establishing pinnipeds as a highly promising model for phonatory production learning, and introduce a new paradigm for systematically assessing respiratory, phonatory and filter control across species.
records.title: Supplementary material from "Learning without a model: extensive phonatory control in a semi-aquatic mammal"

records.abstract: This project will expand the scope of the Alaska Native Harbor Seal Commission's (ANHSC) present biological sampling efforts to include subsistence hunters in communities west of Prince William Sound. The Commission is a tribal consortium concerned with self-management of the harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) as a subsistence resource. The ANHSC already conducts a biological sampling program in nine communities and participates in the harvest data assessment program with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game Subsistence Division. We plan to expand this effort to nine more communities in western Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. Local technicians are selected and trained by the Commission's staff to perform basic necropsies on seals taken by subsistence hunters. Samples from these seals are sent to the University of Alaska Museum (UAM) for distribution to ongoing investigations and for archiving in the permanent collections. Tissue samples will be archived in the Alaska Frozen Tissue Collection (AFTC) which has become the primary regional archive for frozen zoological samples and a major contributor to environmental studies of the North Pacific and Arctic oceans. It is now the world's third largest frozen tissue collection for wild mammals (Hafner et al. 1997). The increasingly powerful tools of molecular biology and biochemistry and the need to monitor perturbation of the environment are accelerating both collection growth and usage. In addition to supporting expanded monitoring and sampling by the ANHSC, this project supports additional student help at UAM to process the increased number of samples. This project will increase the scope of sampling from a protected and potentially threatened high-trophic-level subsistence resource, and increase the scope of Native involvement in the study and management of marine resources. This project also includes; Gordon Jarrell, University of Alaska Fairbanks, P.O. Box 757220, Fairbanks, Alaska 99775-7220, fnghj@uaf.edu Monica Riedel, Alaska Native Harbor Seal Commission, P.O. records.abstract: Protected areas are expected to provide suitable habitats for wildlife even within human-altered landscapes, but environmental cues can be misleading. We evaluated whether a strictly protected, rehabilitated marshland (Kis-Balaton, KB) acts as an ecological trap for the Eurasian otter ( Lutra lutra ), a sentinel apex predator. Using non-invasive genetic sampling within the marshland (90 individuals) and nationwide post-mortem monitoring (462 individuals), we found a spatially heterogeneous population, with a genetically insulated peripheral group. Kinship and group sex ratios indicated kin-structured residents, among which frequent attack-related injuries were consistent with strong territorial behaviour. Net gene flow was directed towards the marshland's core area, mainly via the Zala River. However, immigrants were mainly detected in peripheral areas near settlements and roads, where recovered carcasses showed a higher prevalence of attack-related injuries (KB: 35.7%, other regions: 13.1%), and body condition was poorer in injured than in uninjured otters. These patterns indicate that immigrants rarely integrate into the resident population. The core population remains demographically viable, so the marshland is not a classical ecological trap but a dead-end for dispersers rather than a true refuge. Failure of immigrants to establish, despite apparent habitat connectivity, suggests intrinsic constraints that may be set by the area's ecological carrying capacity. We recommend restoring habitat connectivity, improving legal protection and suitability of small watercourses, and implementing road mitigation and free-ranging dog control to reduce mortality risks. These actions are crucial for gene flow and long-term otter population viability in wetland ecosystems.
records.title: All that glitters is not gold: genetic and post-mortem monitoring indicate dispersal risks for a semi-aquatic apex predator in a protected marshland

records.abstract: During the late summer of 1997, for the first time ever recorded, most of the continental shelf of the eastern Bering Sea was covered by aquamarine waters (Figure 1) which resulted from a massive bloom of coccolithophores (Figure 2). Reflectance of light off the calcium carbonate plates of the flagellated coccolithophores gave the water its anomalous color, which was first observed in July. The bloom was also clearly visible from space, as shown by some of the first images from the multispectral SeaWiFS scanner in September. Light penetration into the water column, essential for primary production by diatoms and other Phytoplankton, was markedly reduced. This shift in the dominant primary producers potentially altered the trophic dynamics throughout the food web of one of world's most productive ecosystems. Prior to and during the bloom, anomalous atmospheric and oceanic conditions were evident. In July, large whales were relatively abundant in the region of the middle shelf where the bloom occurred. Concomitant with the bloom of coccolithophores were die offs of seabirds and a decrease in the number of salmon returning to Bristol Bay. Reports of die-offs of seabirds began in early August. Field operations conducted as part of the National Science Foundation's Inner Front project and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Coastal Ocean Program and Fisheries Oceanography Coordinated Investigations provide a wealth of data to explore this year's anomalous conditions. The eastern Bering Sea shelf (Figure 3) consists of domains characterized by water properties, water column structure and plankton dynamics. Coastal water (depth less than 50 m) is typically mixed by a combination of tidal and wind stirring. Water over the middle shelf (depth 50-100 m) usually has two well mixed layers: the upper a result of the annual melt of sea ice and/or solar heating while the lower remains cold and rich in nutrients essential for Phytoplankton growth. Separating the domains is a structure or inner front which extends for over 1000 km around the shelf. The dynamics of the inner front likely provide nitrogenous nutrients for the prolonged primary and secondary production which typically occurs there. Typical springtime Phytoplankton blooms in the Bering Sea are comprised of diatoms and are associated with increased water column stratification as a result of sea-ice meltback or solar radiation. Summertime Phytoplankton blooms of the magnitude observed this year are rare, in part because the nutrients for plant growth are generally thought to be limiting. Zooplankton biomass may be enhanced two different ways: increased secondary production via increased food availability for herbivorous grazers, and physical concentration of grazers due to convergence of water at the front. As a result of the favorable conditions generated by this increase in prey biomass, massive flocks of seabirds return each year to feed at the front and breed in Alaskan waters. A sequence of unusual phenomena occurred in the coupled atmosphere-ice-ocean system this year which may have favored rapid growth of the coccolithophores. Winter sea ice conditions exhibited average areal and latitudinal extent but melt back appeared to be unusually rapid. In spring and summer, there were reduced numbers of energetic storms and anomalously cloud free conditions. One consequence was that greater stratification than usual occurred over the shelf. Sea surface temperatures were up to 3￸ C above normal in June. The decrease in storms and clouds resulted from atmospheric connections to the current El Nino occurring in the equatorial Pacific. The warm waters were not due to a direct oceanic connection to the ongoing El Nino. Aquamarine waters were first observed in early July. By this time, the normal summer Phytoplankton community had probably been replaced by coccolithophores. Characteristic of these blooms is surface waters that have high reflectance, low chlorophyll and particulate organic carbon concentrations. Light penetration and visibility in the aquamarine waters were markedly reduced, with Secchi depths of one-third normal being observed (2 meters in bloom areas versus about 6 meters in non-bloom areas). Light extinction coefficients at Nunivak Island, as determined by the PAR sensor on the CTD (conductivity, temperature, depth measurements), doubled from June to August (0.07/meter in June and 0.14/meter in August). By September, the areal extent of the bloom was 700x300 kilometers. The vertical extent of the bloom, based on underwater video observations made in September, varied from a thin layer to a layer up to 50 meters deep. In some areas near shore the layer extended to the sea floor. At that time the bloom had been evident for two months which is longer than most recorded blooms. The conditions near the inner front off Cape Newenham provide an example of the abnormal conditions. In June, nitrogenous nutrients were depleted from the bottom layer of the middle shelf and the inner front was not well developed. Short-tailed shearwaters (Puffinus tenuirostris), however, were eating their normal diet of adult euphausiids and had normal body weights. In mid-July, densities of seabirds were lower in the eastern edge of the aquamarine waters of outer Bristol Bay. In general, however, the condition and behavior of pelagic seabirds was normal during July. Large feeding flocks of short-tailed shearwaters were observed on the middle shelf. By the first week of August, coastal die-offs of birds were reported. During the late summer and early fall, a major die-off occurred with thousands of dead birds washing ashore. In the fall, observations near the Pribilof Islands and off Nunivak Island substantiated the reports. Corpses of birds were conspicuous in areas affected by the bloom. Both dead and living shearwaters had significantly reduced body mass compared to birds collected in June, indicating starvation. In addition to the typical diet for shearwaters in Bristol Bay of euphausiids, fish and squid were also being ingested. Those birds ingesting euphausiids were preying upon the smaller juvenile stages. Additionally, foraging shearwaters appeared to avoid areas with aquamarine water (both around the inner fronts and at the Pribilof Islands), where they may have had difficulty in detecting and capturing prey under the existing low underwater light conditions. Given the observations to date, we believe starvation was the prime cause of the shearwater die-off. Other changes were evident in the ecosystem. The Bristol Bay salmon run was at least 15 million fish below predictions. Evidence from a test fishery at Port Moller suggests that the fish were dying on their way to Bristol Bay. Salmon were found to be more common in the diets of the northern fur seal than in previous years. Redistributions of some species of whales in the southeast Bering Sea may have occurred, but there are few large-scale synoptic surveys of cetaceans available for comparison during the past 20 years. During July, five species of large whales (humpback whales - Megaptera novaeangliae, fin whale - Balaenoptera physalus, sei whale - Balaenoptera borealis, minke whale - Balaenoptera acutorostrata, and right whale - Eubalaena glacialis) and harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) were observed either in or near the coccolithophore bloom on the middle shelf. This suggests that the bloom and adjacent waters provided productive foraging for cetaceans and their prey. Comparison of this year with more normal years in the future will be needed to confirm the changes in feeding behavior. records.abstract: This project will expand the scope of the Alaska Native Harbor Seal Commission's (ANHSC) present biological sampling efforts to include subsistence hunters in communities west of Prince William Sound. The Commission is a tribal consortium concerned with self-management of the harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) as a subsistence resource. The ANHSC already conducts a biological sampling program in nine communities and participates in the harvest data assessment program with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game Subsistence Division. We plan to expand this effort to nine more communities in western Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. Local technicians are selected and trained by the Commission's staff to perform basic necropsies on seals taken by subsistence hunters. Samples from these seals are sent to the University of Alaska Museum (UAM) for distribution to ongoing investigations and for archiving in the permanent collections. Tissue samples will be archived in the Alaska Frozen Tissue Collection (AFTC) which has become the primary regional archive for frozen zoological samples and a major contributor to environmental studies of the North Pacific and Arctic oceans. It is now the world's third largest frozen tissue collection for wild mammals (Hafner et al. 1997). The increasingly powerful tools of molecular biology and biochemistry and the need to monitor perturbation of the environment are accelerating both collection growth and usage. In addition to supporting expanded monitoring and sampling by the ANHSC, this project supports additional student help at UAM to process the increased number of samples. This project will increase the scope of sampling from a protected and potentially threatened high-trophic-level subsistence resource, and increase the scope of Native involvement in the study and management of marine resources. This project also includes; Gordon Jarrell, University of Alaska Fairbanks, P.O. Box 757220, Fairbanks, Alaska 99775-7220, fnghj@uaf.edu Monica Riedel, Alaska Native Harbor Seal Commission, P.O. records.abstract: Human activities and their pressuresFishing poses the highest impact risk to ecosystem state components through selective extraction of species, physical seabed disturbance, incidental bycatch, and marine litter resulting from abandoned, lost, or discarded fishing gear (ALDFG).Fishing intensity has declined over the past two decades with the implementation of harvest control measures.Widely distributed pelagic stocks continue to experience fishing mortality above FMSY because of the absence of coastal state agreements. This poses a risk to long-term sustainability.Fishery closures have been established that are a step toward protecting the ecoregion’s diverse benthic habitats and vulnerable marine ecosystems (VME) from disturbance by bottom-contacting fishing gear.To a lesser extent, wastewater and shipping pose a risk to all ecosystem components by releasing marine litter, namely microplastics and other contaminants.The risks posed by wastewater are aggravated by limited wastewater treatment infrastructures. Pressures associated with shipping are anticipated to increase in the ecoregion.State of the ecosystemPrimary production is high in Icelandic waters, and phytoplankton biomass is increasing on the south Iceland shelf.Stocks of northern shrimp (Pandalus borealis), Norway lobster (Nephrops norvegicus), Atlantic halibut (Hippoglossus hippoglossus), and beaked redfish (Sebastes mentella) remain below historical biomass levels, while the biomasses of mackerel (Scomber scombrus) and Norwegian spring spawning herring (Clupea harengus) are below target.Populations of fulmars (Fulmarus glacialis) and kittiwakes (Rissa tridactyla) continue to decline in the ecoregion.The status of harbour seal (Phoca vitulina) remains a conservation concern in the ecoregion.Recent changes in capelin (Mallotus villosus) abundance and distribution are expected to have important consequences on Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), seabirds, and whales in the ecoregion.Climate changeSurface and bottom waters of the Iceland shelf have warmed by > 1.1°C since 1975, primarily due to increased northward transport of Atlantic Water into the ecoregion.Warming is most pronounced in surface waters in the north, where a shift in zooplankton community composition from Arctic to boreal large copepod taxa is evident.Rising temperatures have contributed to the decline of northern shrimp and Iceland scallop (Chlamys islandica) populations, to the shifting capelin distribution beyond the Iceland shelf, and to groundfish species moving northward or to deeper waters.Surface water pH is declining on the shelf. Acidification effects on marine biota and habitats are largely unknown and are a key concern in the ecoregion.Warming is projected to continue and result in the spatial redistribution of commercially harvested species on the Iceland shelf.Environmental and socio-economic contextFisheries significantly contribute to national revenues and employment and have high cultural importance in the ecoregion.Balancing economic and social benefits from fisheries with ecosystem conservation objectives is a key trade-off in the ecoregion.The rapid growth of tourism, shipping, and finfish aquaculture is raising additional societal concerns and trade-offs among marine sectors and associated pressures.

records.abstract: Incidental bycatch of harbour porpoise ( Phocoena phocoena ) in set-net fisheries poses a threat to their populations. Pingers, acoustic devices designed to deter cetaceans, are currently the primary tool used to reduce porpoise bycatch without impeding fishing effort. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of different pinger spacing configurations at reducing porpoise bycatch in the Danish North Sea turbot ( Scophthalmus maximus ) fishery. Three trials were conducted in 2021, 2023, and 2025, testing standard Banana pingers with varying spacings of 200 m and 500 m (B-200 and B-500, respectively), and a third alternative using a louder Banana pinger version (LB-500) with a 500 m spacing. Another, even louder, pinger type (DDDs) was tested only in 2025 with a spacing of 1,800 m. Results from the combined trials indicated that B-200 reduced bycatch per unit effort (BPUE) by 66%, B-500 reduced BPUE by 30% and STM-1800 reduced BPUE by 52%. Across years, pingers showed inconsistent results. B-200 reduced porpoise bycatch by 56% in 2023 and by 73% in 2025, while B-500 reduced bycatch by 55% only in 2025. LB-500 reduced bycatch by 74% in 2025, and STM-1800 reduced bycatch by 64% in 2025. These results show that, while increasing pinger spacing reduces pinger implementation costs, effectiveness declines significantly unless the pinger's source level is increased. This research underscores the need for precise pinger spacing regulations to effectively reduce harbour porpoise bycatch.
records.title: MIND THE GAP: Pingers, spacing, and sound levels influence bycatch rates of harbour porpoises

records.abstract: Introduction: Toxoplasma gondii oocysts shed in the feces of cats and other felids (definitive hosts) are resistant in the environment, particularly in seawater. They can remain infectious for several months and serve as a source of contamination for marine mammals. The objective of our study is to assess the prevalence of T. gondii in marine mammals stranded between 2010 and 2023 on the French metropolitan coasts, and to characterize the genetic diversity of the infecting strains.Materials/Methods: A total of 60 muscle samples were collected, including 43 common dolphins (Delphinus delphis), 6 bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus), 5 harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena), 3 striped dolphins (Stenella coeruleoalba), 1 long-finned pilot whale (Globicephala melas), 1 gray seal (Halichoerus grypus), and 1 Cuvier’s beaked whale (Ziphius cavirostris). A modified agglutination test (MAT) on meat juice and a direct qPCR (529 RE and B1) on DNA extracted from the sampled tissues, were performed, followed by a microsatellite genotyping when possible.Results: The overall seroprevalence was of 56.7% (34/60) with a specific seroprevalence for common dolphins of 69.8% (30/43) while two harbor porpoises and two bottlenose dolphins were seropositive. Quantitative PCR confirmed the presence of T. gondii in 8 of the 30 seropositive common dolphins. Three isolates were genotyped, revealing type II genotypes. By comparing these genotypes with published data and the French National Reference Centre forToxoplasmosis database, the strains were found to be closely related to type II strains isolated from a French and a Turkish patients and a French pig, differing by only 1–3 markers.Conclusions: The high seroprevalence of T. gondii in marine mammals, particularly in common dolphins, suggests significant contamination of the sea by oocysts. The identification of three genotypes belonging to the type II lineage predominant in Europe provides evidence of circulation between terrestrial and marine environment, particularly through the leaching of soil contaminated by feces from infected cats. The results concerning certain species should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of samples, hence the need for a larger study to better understand the risk factors and ecological implications.
records.title: Prevalence and genotypes of Toxoplasma gondii in marine mammals of France

records.abstract: Harbor Porpoises occur regularly in the north Pacific Ocean and the Bering Sea and occasionally in the Chukchi Sea during the ice-free months. Point Barrow, Alaska is considered to be near the northern limit of distribution for this species. We have obtained nine records from the vicinity of Point Barrow between 1985 and 1991. Harbor Porpoises were found entangled in subsistence fishing nets, seen live or found dead on the beach. These records indicate a regular use of the northeastern Chukchi Sea and extreme western Beaufort Sea. The reasons for their occurrence near Point Barrow are unknown but the relative abundance of fish in coastal arctic lagoons may attract Harbor Porpoises northward. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
authors: North Slope Borough Dept. Wildl. Manage.

records.abstract: Uniform format life talbes for seven pinniped species were prepared using previously published data on body mass and natural mortality rates by age. These data were pooled by sex, and a single point estimate of the average body mass for the population was calculated from the life table data. Pinniped species include northern fur seal (Callorhinus ursinus), northern sea lions (Eumetopias jubatus), Pacific harbor seals (Phoca vitulina richardii), spotted seals (Phoca largha), ringed seals (Phoca hispida), ribbon seals (Phoca fasciata), and bearded seals (Erignathus barbatus) in the Bering Sea. records.abstract: ABSTRACT The Eurasian otter ( Lutra lutra ) is a semiaquatic, freshwater top predator of conservation concern due to its significant global population decline in the last century. Following its recovery and recolonization in parts of Europe, the population faces ongoing threats, including habitat loss and fragmentation due to human activities, climate change, prey depletion, and exposure to emerging contaminants. Accurately identifying its diet is crucial for understanding ecological interactions and proposing effective management strategies. DNA metabarcoding based on high‐throughput sequencing is a reliable diet analysis tool with better resolution than traditional methods. This study, for the first time, applied two 16S rRNA primers targeting different prey classes on the dietary spectrum of two Eurasian otters populations returning to Northern Germany (Schleswig‐Holstein and Lower Saxony). DNA fragments of prey items from the gut contents of 156 otters collected between 2005 and 2022 were sequenced. Fifty‐five operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were identified in the dietary remains, including freshwater and marine fish, anurans, caudates, and water birds. Otters in the study area are opportunistic predators with wide dietary plasticity, feeding on the most abundant species. Nine‐spined sticklebacks, common roach, and common frogs were important prey items, and marine fish species were detected in the diet of some of the investigated otters. The otters' diet differed between Lower Saxony and Schleswig‐Holstein, between sexes, and a slight difference was observed between adults and subadults. This study provides new insights into the diet composition of otters and their ability to exploit a variety of resources in their habitat. This information is vital for understanding their chances of survival in an environment that is continuously changing due to human impacts and for developing effective management tools.
records.title: Guts and Glory: Unraveling the Diet of Eurasian Otter ( Lutra lutra ) Populations Using DNA Metabarcoding of Gut Contents

records.abstract: ABSTRACT Kashmir Valley is a unique landscape nestled in the northwest Himalaya. It is a flat‐bottomed valley flanked on all sides by mountains. The valley is drained by the River Jhelum, which is fed by an extensive network of tributaries. The valley was once an uncontested abode of Eurasian otters. However, for the past many decades, no sighting of the animal was reported until recently. Hunting, habitat destruction, and pollution were the main reasons for pushing the population into decline. This paper collates the recent reports of Eurasian Otter sightings from the valley after decades, establishing the re‐emergence of the otters in the valley. This brings a propitious moment for ecological health and resilience. It further outlines the possible threats that have emerged recently and will impact the otter population's re‐emergence severely. The study also highlights the need for conservation to firmly re‐establish otters as top predators of Kashmir's freshwater ecosystems and the means of achieving the otter conservation goals.
records.title: Re‐Emergence of Eurasian Otter ( Lutra Lutra ) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge

records.abstract: Ecological and environmental drivers shape evolution, yet little is known about the molecular underpinnings of adaptation. Omics tools (e.g. genomics and transcriptomics) can help us understand the mechanisms of long-term trait evolution, such as lactation strategies, and shorter-term population dynamics. Pinnipeds (seals, sea lions, fur seals, and walruses), a closely related monophyletic group, represent some of the most extreme and diverse lactation strategies known. This trait diversity stems from their worldwide distribution across a wide range of habitats and latitudes, and their obligate spatiotemporal separation of land and sea for breeding and foraging. In this thesis, we uncover signals of molecular evolution of key lactation traits in pinnipeds using comparative functional genomics and comparative transcriptomics. We identify candidate changes in pathways linked to mammary involution and lipid metabolism, and reveal coordinated expression of genes involved in lipid mobilisation, energy balance, high fat milk, and mother-to-pup energy transfer. Novel grey seal transcriptomes for milk fat, blubber, and pup blubber were generated from collections made in early (day 5) and late (day 15) lactation on the Isle of May 2023. Along with uncovering the protein properties of key milk fat globule membrane genes, we obtained the first physical properties of milk fat globules in grey seals – allowing us to investigate mechanisms of milk emulsion stability in high fat milk. Our findings show that seal milk contains exceptionally small globules with weakened net surface charge, offering a potential mechanism for stabilising high-fat milk. Finally, we reconstructed the demographic history and genetic health of Caspian seals, showing that changes in effective population size track major paleoenvironmental shifts while recent inbreeding remains low, providing direction for future conservation strategies. Overall, the findings presented in this thesis represent an important foundation for future omics studies targeting marine mammal biology, and offer a lens into understanding eco-evolutionary trajectories of populations and extreme phenotypes.

records.title: Genomics approaches to uncovering eco-evolutionary adaptations in pinnipeds

records.abstract: Between October 8 and October 15, 2026, an operational field vehicle operated by MobiCom Corporation—a consolidated Mongolian telecommunications subsidiary of Japan's KDDI Corporation—ignited dry steppe vegetation during fiber-optic border station maintenance in eastern Mongolia's Dornod Province. The resulting wildfire burned approximately 530,000 ha (~5,300 sq km, or 2.4x the area of Metropolitan Tokyo), consuming 79.8% of the Numrug Strictly Protected Area (a critical refuge for Ussuri moose, Eurasian otter, and 263 avian species) and advancing to the Inner Mongolia border of the People's Republic of China, where 606 Mongolian and 3,400 Chinese personnel were mobilized. Treating this ecological catastrophe merely as an unverified Profit-and-Loss (P&L) extraordinary indemnity expense (L_P&L) exposes the parent corporation and Japanese sovereign diplomacy to compounding cross-border geopolitical friction, Mongolian public backlash, and severe Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) penalties under Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) LEAP and Sustainability Standards Board of Japan (SSBJ) statutory filings. Building directly upon the sovereign agro-ecological architecture established in Zenodo Monograph 10.5281/zenodo.23654305, this monograph formulates a deterministic four-pillar Sovereign Nature-Positive Restoration Protocol tailored to the Mongolian steppe ecosystem. First, we prove Theorem 2.1 (Steppe Balance-Sheet Environmental Assetization), converting deadweight P&L indemnity losses into capitalized Balance-Sheet (B/S) ecological restoration infrastructure assets (Delta A_env) coupled with Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) Methodology JP-MN-STEPPE-01 for rotational grazing and Soil Organic Carbon (Delta C_SOC) sequestration bundled with nomadic "Five Snouts" (Tavan Khoshuu Mal, H_k) polygon traceability (P_k). Second, we formalize a Sovereign Digital Public Goods Barter deploying Japan's JAXA ALOS-4 (DAICHI-4) PALSAR-3 L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (200 km swath, 3 m resolution) to penetrate smoke and cloud cover, providing the Mongolian Ministry of Environment and Climate Change with cryptographic burn-severity mapping and neutralizing cross-border disinformation while executing Paris Agreement Article 6.2 Corresponding Adjustments (alpha_ITMO). Third, we embed deterministic hardware interlocks (PHOENIX_BRIDGE x QFS-zkVM over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field F_p, p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1) into maintenance vehicles and telecom base stations, enforcing sub-0.5 ms RTO P2.0 thermal/geofence ignition cutoffs and 2/3 Human-in-Command (HIC) threshold authorization. Fourth, we establish Proposition 5.1 and Theorem 5.1, proving how zero-knowledge spatial verification (rho_verified -> 1) eliminates the SSBJ/TNFD unverified risk multiplier (kappa_penalty >= 4.0) and satisfies board fiduciary oversight mandates under Delaware Caremark and Japan's Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA). records.abstract: The Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra), a semi-aquatic carnivore listed as “Near Threatened” by the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature), is widespread across Eurasia but remains poorly studied genetically in various regions. We analyzed the Central Anatolian population along the Kızılırmak River using mitochondrial (mt) DNA from non-invasively collected samples to examine whether Anatolian otters connect phylogenetically typical European and Caucasian lineages and whether Anatolia could have harbored a late-glacial source population for otter migration to Europe via western (Balkan) and/or eastern (east of the Black Sea) routes. Thirty spraints were collected from five localities, including four previously known sites and one newly identified in the Sulakyurt district, northeast of Kırıkkale province. We amplified a short (256 bp) mtD-loop fragment and a longer (820 bp) fragment spanning the Cytb, tRNA-Thr, tRNA-Pro, and D-loop from 14 samples and included all corresponding Lutra lutra mtDNA sequences available in GenBank in our analyses. Six short-fragment samples from Kapulukaya, Kesikköprü, and Kalecik carried the widespread northern Eurasian haplotype Lut1, while eight samples from Kalecik, Kesikköprü, Hirfanlı, and Hamzalı revealed a novel haplotype (H256-TR). The long fragments represented two additional haplotypes (H820-37, H820-38), distributed across the same localities. Median-joining network analysis of the short fragment produced a star-like topology with no clear phylogeographic structuring, whereas the longer fragment resolved two weakly separated phylogenetic groups. Central Anatolian haplotypes were positioned between Far Eastern and northern Eurasian lineages, with H820-38 phylogenetically connecting Caucasian and European haplotypes. This finding is consistent with the hypothesis of possible western and eastern postglacial migration routes from Anatolia to Europe, although broader spatial sampling is needed for confirmation.
records.title: Mitochondrial DNA Lineages of Eurasian Otters (Lutra lutra) in Central Anatolia: A Phylogenetic Bridge Between Asia and Europe?

records.abstract: The harbor seal ( Phoca vitulina ) is a sentinel top predator in the North Sea, inhabiting regions with high shipping activity. The rapid expansion of offshore wind farms (OWFs) is expected to further increase vessel traffic and underwater noise levels. The population-relevant behavioral consequences for harbor seals remain difficult to infer from tagging or visual surveys alone due to limited sample sizes, uneven coverage, and strong interindividual variability. This chapter presents a methodological framework that couples a large-scale, time-varying vessel noise soundscape with a telemetry-informed agent-based model (ABM) to explore potential future scenarios and mitigation efforts. Behavioral parameters were derived from 13 seals equipped with sound and movement sensing biologgers (DTAGs). Simulated animals were programmed with empirically derived parameters within four defined behavioral states, while the behavioral response functions are integrated as state-probability modifiers. Four scenarios are defined: a 2018 baseline, OWF-2030 and OWF-2050 traffic projections, and a speed-reduction policy within marine protected areas. The chapter provides a reproducible blueprint for constructing, parameterizing, and coupling soundscape and ABM components, enabling transparent what-if analyses beyond the reach of observational studies.
records.title: Harbor Seal Behavior Under Shipping Noise: A Coupled Soundscape and Agent-Based Modeling Approach

records.abstract: The effect of a pinger designed to reduce cetacean bycatch in fisheries on the behavior of a harbor porpoise was quantified through exposure experiments in a pool. The “banana pinger” (Fishtek Marine Ltd.) sounds were comprised of signal blocks (duration ~0.5 s), each containing four frequency components (8–125 kHz; peak 70 kHz). Sounds were played back at mean received levels of 83, 89, 95, 101, and 107 dB re 1 μPa. Behavioral responses, including increased respiration rate, jumping, and swimming faster and farther away from the source, occurred from 95 dB re 1 μPa. At sea, distances at which harbor porpoises are deterred by pingers will depend on environmental parameters influencing sound propagation. Based on this study with a captive individual, wild porpoises should hear the “banana pinger” sounds at a greater distance than the deterring distance, so sounds may alert them and reduce their likelihood of entanglement. Pingers should be easy to use, reliable, and durable. Cost, sound pollution, directionality, habituation, and audibility to seals and fish should be minimized; range and deterring effect should be optimized. Due to its behavioral effect on harbor porpoises, the “banana pinger” appears to be effective.
records.title: Reducing Fisheries Bycatch: Behavioral Responses of a Harbor Porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) in a Pool to the Sounds of a “Banana Pinger”

records.abstract: The first large scale decommissioning projects of offshore wind farms are planned in Europe in the coming 5 years. The underwater sound generated during the decommissioning phase of offshore wind farms remains poorly understood due to the limited number of such projects conducted to date. Nevertheless, activities associated with decommissioning have the potential to impact marine life. This study is the first to present acoustic effect ranges from decommissioning activities associated with the removal of a 1.8 m diameter monopile by abrasive cutting and assessing their potential impact on the harbour porpoise. Two JASCO Multi-Channel Acoustic Recorders, equipped with two hydrophones, were deployed for ~10 days in November 2024. The potential impact ranges on relevant marine fauna calculated for three key operations were studied: jacking-up of the vessel, dredging down-the-hole and cutting. The permanent threshold shift onset threshold was never exceeded by any of the operations. Both dredging and cutting exceeded the VHF weighted temporary threshold shift (TTS, L E = 153 dB re 1 μPa 2 s according to Southall et al. (2019) and 161 dB re 1 μPa 2 s according to the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS).
records.title: Store Middelgrund Monopile Removal: How Far Can Sound Emissions from Decommissioning Impact on the Harbour Porpoise?

records.abstract: Offshore wind farm construction requires regulatory assessment of the numbers of marine mammals at risk of auditory injury or disturbance from impulsive piling noise. However, there is high uncertainty within assessment frameworks, and limited opportunities to validate outputs. Here monitoring data collected during construction of Moray West Offshore Wind Farm were used to compare measurements of: (1) underwater noise and (2) harbor porpoise behavioral responses with predictions made during regulatory assessments. Noise measurements were made during the installation of 13 monopiles and harbor porpoise responses to pile driving at seven sites were monitored using an array of echolocation detectors (CPODs). Measured maximum received noise levels were 177–181 dB re 1μPa 2 s (SEL ss ) at 750 m. Measurements were typically within 1 dB (range −2.4 dB to +3 dB) of values predicted from acoustic modelling. Responses of porpoises to monopile installation were similar to those observed in earlier studies of pin-piling at the adjacent Beatrice Offshore Wind Farm despite observed noise levels being much higher at Moray West. Together, these results provide confidence in current approaches to acoustic modelling but highlight that existing approaches to estimating disturbance to cetaceans from impact piling in UK waters are likely conservative.
records.title: Measurements of Noise Levels and Porpoise Disturbance During Pile-Driving at Moray West Wind Farm: Comparison with Model Predictions Used in Regulatory Assessments

records.abstract: The Dogger Bank, a shallow sandbank in the center of the North Sea, has a valuable status as a Special Area of Conservation (SAC) and an Important Marine Mammal Area (IMMA). However, the region faces increasing amounts of anthropogenic activity and the produced underwater noise may affect sound-sensitive species, such as the harbor porpoise. This study presents findings from a short-term passive acoustic monitoring campaign (July–November 2024) conducted in the northwest corner of the Dogger Bank, addressing the previous lack of sound data available in this remote region. Daily median sound pressure levels ranged between 97 and 109 dB re 1 μPa, with ship passages and geophysical survey sounds causing transient spikes in sound pressure levels below 1 kHz. Natural drivers of variability were also examined, revealing a positive correlation between wind speed and sound levels above 800 Hz. In terms of biological detections, 23% of recordings contained high-frequency clicks classified as harbor porpoise. Fish and minke whale vocalizations were also manually identified. The data recorded provided new insights into the soundscape of this internationally recognized marine mammal habitat, the first step in understanding how anthropogenic activity may alter sound levels from baseline and the degree of mitigation required.
records.title: Exploring the Marine Soundscape of the Dogger Bank

records.abstract: Floating Offshore Wind (FOW) will soon add significant capacity to the renewable energy sector. However, data gaps remain with respect to potential environmental risks of these installations. Operational noise from FOW will produce continuous underwater noise over decades to come. While noise signatures from fixed-bottom turbines are well understood, there is uncertainty regarding the noise profile and potential impacts of FOW turbines. Here, two FOW farms were acoustically surveyed, one with semi-submersible (Kincardine) and one with floating spar (Hywind Scotland) systems. Similar to operational noise of fixed turbines, FOW noise emissions were mostly below 200 Hz and exhibited distinct tonal features between 50 and 80 Hz at Kincardine, and 25 and 75 Hz at Hywind Scotland. The sound pressure levels 100 m from the turbines related to drivetrain vibration and were comparable to sound pressure levels from fixed bottom turbines. In addition, temporally intermittent broadband transients, which were thought to be related to the mooring systems, were recorded at both systems. Harbor porpoise detections were lower at 300–600 m from the turbines compared to 1500–2400 m at both FOW sites. This work highlights cumulative operational noise of large FOW arrays as a potential stressor to the marine environment. Where possible, effective mitigation options should be investigated.
records.title: Underwater Noise Produced by Two Types of Operational Floating Wind Turbines and Preliminary Data on Harbor Porpoise Responses

records.abstract: This dataset contains derived biologging metrics from 28 harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) tagged with DTAGs in the Kattegat and Belt Sea between 2012 and 2023. For each deployment, the dataset provides buzz count (used to derive buzz rate, a proxy for prey-capture attempts and energy acquisition) and respiration count (used to derive respiration rate, a proxy for energy expenditure) recorded during day and night periods under two treatment conditions: control (background noise) and exposure to vessel noise exceeding 97 dB re 1 µPa (VHF cetacean-weighted). These derived metrics were used to quantify the effects of vessel noise on harbour porpoise foraging behaviour and energy budgets, as reported in Rojano-Doñate et al. (2026, PNAS). A README file describes all variables and units.

records.abstract: In June 2020, JASCO Applied Sciences undertook a sound source characterization (SSC) study of a geophysical seabed survey at the planned North Sea Energy Island site, Denmark. These surveys use multiple types of sound sources to image the seabed, including sparkers, parametric sonars, sub-bottom profilers (SBPs), side-scan sonars, and ultrashort baseline positioning systems (USBL). This is the first dedicated study aimed at characterizing each of the sources involved with a typical geophysics survey of this type. Individual passes were recorded at multiple distances out to 10 km for the sources alone and in combination with the same distribution and settings as they would usually be deployed for such a survey. The pass in the vessel’s typical configuration with all sources active was evaluated against the Southall et al. (Aquat Mamm 45(2):125–232, 2019) thresholds’ acoustic effect criteria for VHF cetaceans and the harbor porpoise behavioral threshold (Tougaard, Thresholds for behavioral responses to noise in marine mammals: background note to revision of guidelines from the Danish Energy Agency. Document Number 225. Technical report by Aarhus University, Department of Ecoscience for Danish Centre for Environment and Energy (DCE). 32p. https://dce2.au.dk/pub/TR225.pdf, 2021). The results showed that the PTS threshold of 173 dB re 1 μPa 2 s for the SEL is exceeded within less than 5 m from the source; the TTS threshold of 153 dB re 1 μPa 2 s for the SEL is exceeded within ~250 m from the source. The sound levels for all sources combined fell below a VHF-weighted sound pressure level 100 dB re 1 μPa L p125ms at ~11 km from the source.
records.title: Underwater Sound Signatures from Geophysics Survey Spread: Case Study from the North Sea Energy Island, Denmark

records.abstract: A significant quantity of unexploded ordnance (UXO) lies on the North Sea seabed. Uncontrolled detonations of these wartime relics pose severe risk, including fatalities to both humans and marine life; consequently, their presence is a matter of grave concern, necessitating removal. This study is the first to examine impacts of high-order UXO detonations on the behavioral response of harbor porpoises based on in situ data. Impacts were evaluated for four UXOs at the East Anglia ONE wind farm (southern North Sea) detonated without noise abatement. Impacts were most substantial for the heaviest UXO (1000 lb), where porpoise occurrence and presence of echolocation buzzes, indicative of potential foraging behavior, were substantially reduced after detonation compared to before out to a distance of 15–20 km. In contrast, increased porpoise detection and buzz rates were found beyond this distance when assessed over increasingly longer periods, suggesting displacement of individuals. While impacts from detonations could not be disentangled from related detonation activities, e.g., vessel presence, acoustic deterrent device activation, and fish scaring charges detonation, results show that the overall high-order UXO detonation process can result in porpoise displacement and impact potential foraging activity. Further empirical research on behavior responses to UXO clearances is urgently needed.
records.title: Impact of High-Order Unexploded Bomb Clearance on Harbor Porpoise Presence

records.abstract: Climate change poses a significant threat to global biodiversity, particularly in intermittent Mediterranean ecosystems, such as streams, by intensifying drought periods and flooding limiting water availability.The current study investigated the spatio-temporal patterns exhibited by Lutra lutra within riparian systems and the environmental and anthropogenic factors that may exert influence on these patterns. A total of 23 camera traps were set along mediterranean streams, 500 meters distance from each one, from October 2024 until June 2025. Temporal patterns of activity were estimated using kernel density estimators, Rayleigh tests, overlap coefficient analysis and Watson-Wheeler for test similarity in patterns between different environmental contexts. The evaluation of spatial patterns’ determinants was conducted using occupancy and N-Mixture models, which incorporated variables such as the physical characteristics of the stream, vegetation structure, and human disturbance. The results indicated trends in activity patterns, with otters showing a nocturnal behaviour with some variation according to the environmental context, although these trends did not reach statistical significance; these were elevated activity levels during nocturnal periods coinciding with periods of reduced moonlight, more intense and brief activity peaks in cold periods, and adjustments in activity times in response to human disturbance. The spatial detection process was found to be influenced by various environmental factors, including the depth and width of the stream, riverbank height, and extent of canopy cover, but none of the tested drivers seemed to affect the occupancy patterns contrarily to the presence of fallen logs that was found to be positively correlated with the abundance of otters. These fallen logs provided structures that facilitated hunting, movement, rest, and recreation behaviours. The results demonstrated the species' capacity for adaptation to diverse environmental conditions and provided indispensable information for conservation strategies, thereby contributing to the sustainable management of streams and the preservation of this species and local biodiversity.

records.abstract: O termo “arrojamento” (em inglês stranding) refere-se à chegada à costa de animais aquáticos mortos ou incapazes de regressar ao mar por si próprios (Geraci and Lounsbury, 1993). Estes eventos, que há séculos despertam o interesse tanto do público como da comunidade científica, constituem oportunidades de amostragem valiosas, que de outra forma seriam logisticamente inviáveis, financeiramente dispendiosas ou eticamente problemáticas. Os arrojamentos fornecem dados fundamentais sobre a diversidade de espécies, os estados de saúde das populações e as pressões persistentes nos ecossistemas (Peltier et al., 2012; GómezHernández et al., 2021). Atualmente, os principais fatores de ameaça à megafauna marinha incluem as alterações climáticas (nomeadamente o aquecimento, a acidificação e a desoxigenação dos oceanos), a poluição e a sobrepesca. Estas pressões, muitas delas interligadas, têm levado muitas espécies ao risco de extinção (Herr et al., 2014; Wernberg et al., 2016; Dulvy et al., 2021). Nesta dissertação, eu foco-me em três principais grupos taxonómicos de megafauna marinha: mamíferos marinhos, tartarugas marinhas e elasmobrânquios (tubarões e raias). Dentro dos mamíferos marinhos, distinguem-se cinco subgrupos principais: odontocetos (baleias de dentes), misticetos (baleias de bossas), pinípedes (focas, leões-marinhos e morsas), sirénios (manatins e dugongos) e lontras-marinhas. Além de ser animais icónicos, também desempenham um papel crucial nas redes tróficas oceânicas. Muitos realizam migrações oceânicas de longa distância, atravessando bacias oceânicas e conectando diferentes ecossistemas, servindo como vetores de transferência de energia, nutrientes e carbono (Block et al., 2011; Estes et al., 2016). Como predadores de topo, exercem controlo "top-down", mantendo o ecossistema em equilíbrio (Estes et al., 2016; Pimiento et al., 2020). Caracterizadas por ciclos de vida lentos, as populações da megafauna recuperam-se lentamente de perturbações (Duarte et al., 2020). A monitorização sistemática dos arrojamentos tem sido identificada como uma prioridade para a investigação marinha e conservação dos oceanos (Clarke et al., 2021), e redes de monitorização têm vindo a crescer em várias regiões do mundo (Pyenson, 2010). Contudo, os padrões globais e as causas subjacentes aos arrojamentos nunca tinham sido avaliados de forma abrangente e sistemática. Para colmatar estas lacunas, o presente estudo oferece uma análise sistemática dos arrojamentos globais de megafauna marinha, identificando os grupos taxonómicos e espécies mais frequentemente envolvidos, as causas subjacentes dos arrojamentos e os principais hotspots globais. Seguindo as diretrizes PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses), foram realizadas três revisões sistemáticas independentes na base de dados Web of Science, uma para cada grupo taxonómico. As pesquisas abrangeram o período entre 1900 e 30 de junho de 2023 e resultaram na criação de três bases de dados globais de arrojamentos. Para os mamíferos marinhos, a pesquisa inicial identificou 2045 publicações, das quais 642 foram incluídas após aplicação de vários critérios de elegibilidade. No caso das tartarugas marinhas, 142 artigos foram selecionados de um total de 610, enquanto a pesquisa sobre elasmobrânquios resultou em 35 artigos elegíveis, a partir de 205. A base de dados compilada integrou informações sobre o número de indivíduos arrojados por espécie, localização e data, e, quando disponíveis, sexo, estádio de desenvolvimento e causa de arrojamento (COS, do inglês cause of stranding). A atribuição geográfica dos arrojamentos foi feita com base em ecorregiões marinhas (Spalding et al., 2007), privilegiando uma abordagem biogeográfica em detrimento da tradicional divisão por fronteiras políticas ou zonas económicas exclusivas. As causas de arrojamento foram padronizadas em 15 categorias aplicáveis aos três grupos. Entre as causas antropogénicas incluíram-se: interação com pescarias, emalhamento, colisão com embarcações, ingestão de lixo marinho, exposição a ruído, trauma causado antropogenicamente e intoxicação pelo florescimento de algas nocivas (HABs). As causas naturais abrangeram doenças, emaciação, predação, problemas reprodutivos e alterações ambientais. Para explorar a relação entre o esforço de monitorização e o número de arrojamentos registados, foi aplicado um modelo estatístico Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial, com o número de redes de monitorização ativas por unidade espacial como variável preditora (Perumean-Chaney et al., 2013). O modelo revelou uma correlação significativa entre a presença de redes de arrojamento ativas e os dados de presença/ausência de arrojamentos, mas não entre as redes e o número total de arrojamentos registados. No total, foram registados mais de 400,000 arrojamentos. Os mamíferos marinhos representaram 66%, seguidos pelas tartarugas marinhas (33%) e pelos elasmobrânquios (1%). As espécies mais frequentemente arrojadas foram a tartaruga-verde (Chelonia mydas, n ~ 70,000) e a tartaruga-comum (Caretta caretta, n ~ 35,000). Entre os mamíferos, destacaram-se o leão-marinho-da-Califórnia (Zalophus californianus, n ~ 27,400), a toninha-comum (Phocoena phocoena, n ~ 26,700) e a foca-comum (Phoca vitulina, n ~ 23,900). No total, os mamíferos marinhos arrojados englobaram 115 espécies diferentes. Os odontocetos (n ~ 24,300) foram o subgrupo com mais registos, seguidos dos pinípedes (n ~ 88,600). Os sirénios, misticetos e mustelídeos (lontras-marinhas) apresentaram números significativamente mais baixos, representando 4%, 2% e 1% dos arrojamentos de mamíferos, respetivamente. As sete espécies existentes de tartarugas marinhas estiveram representadas, bem como 97 espécies de elasmobrânquios. As análises demográficas revelaram variações marcantes entre grupos. Entre todos os mamíferos marinhos com identificação de sexo, observou-se um viés para o sexo masculino (56%). Pelo contrário, nas tartarugas (com exceção de C. caretta), predominavam as fêmeas (61%). Nos elasmobrânquios, a distribuição sexual foi aproximadamente equilibrada (52% fêmeas, 48% machos). Quanto aos estádios de desenvolvimento, a maioria dos mamíferos foi classificada como juvenis/sub-adultos (42%), adultos (31%), crias (23%) e neonatos/fetos (4%). As tartarugas eram predominantemente juvenis (75%), com adultos a representar 21% e sub-adultos 4%. Nos elasmobrânquios, 91% dos indivíduos arrojados eram juvenis, 8% adultos e 1% fetos abortados. Apenas se conseguiu atribuir uma causa definitiva de arrojamento (COS) em 15% dos casos, refletindo limitações logísticas, o estado de decomposição das carcaças e a necessidade de análises detalhadas, como necrópsias e exames laboratoriais. Globalmente, 59% dos arrojamentos com COS atribuída foram causados por atividades humanas. As principais causas foram interação com pescarias (24%), alterações ambientais (22%) e colisões com embarcações (15%), seguidas por doenças e outras causas antropogénicas. No caso das tartarugas marinhas, a principal causa identificada foram as alterações ambientais (48%), em particular episódios de hipotermia aguda induzida por descidas bruscas da temperatura da água (“cold stunning”). A nível geográfico, os registos foram enviesados para o hemisfério norte. A ecorregião Norte da Califórnia destacou-se como o principal hotspot, com cerca de 50,000 arrojamentos — maioritariamente leõesmarinhos da Califórnia (Z. californianus) e outros pinípedes. Seguiu-se a ecorregião do norte do Golfo do México (Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama e norte da Florida), com ~48,000 arrojamentos, dos quais 68% eram mamíferos e 32% tartarugas. No hemisfério sul, o maior número de arrojamentos foi registado na região sudeste do Brasil (estados de São Paulo, Paraná e Santa Catarina), com aproximadamente 27,400 casos, sobretudo de C. mydas. Na Europa, o principal hotspot foi o Mar do Norte, dominado por Phocoena phocoena e Phoca vitulina. Este estudo expandiu, pela primeira vez, o conhecimento sobre os arrojamentos de megafauna marinha, passando de uma perspetiva regional para uma visão global. Identificaram-se padrões geográficos, taxonómicos e demográficos, bem como as principais causas de arrojamento. Este trabalho preenche várias lacunas científicas e fornece uma base sólida para investigações futuras e para a definição de estratégias de conservação e gestão. Face à multiplicidade de ameaças enfrentadas por estas espécies icónicas e ao seu elevado valor ecológico e simbólico, este estudo reforça a importância da monitorização sistemática das praias e do fortalecimento das redes regionais de arrojamento como ferramentas essenciais para a conservação da biodiversidade marinha.

records.abstract: Among small cetaceans, the family Phocoenidae faces critical global conservation challenges, with several species and subpopulations highly threatened by anthropogenic pressures. The Iberian harbour porpoise has been proposed as a subspecies (Phocoena phocoena meridionalis). This genetically distinct and highly threatened population is currently classified as critically endangered in Portugal and endangered in Spain. Strandings data collected over more than two decades (2000–2023), integrated with aerial surveys conducted between 2011 and 2015, 2016 and more recently in 2022 and 2023, allowed for insights into the Iberian harbour porpoise population dynamics and anthropogenic pressures. Between the years 2000 and 2020, porpoise strandings in Portuguese and Galician coasts increased progressively with 47% of analysed individuals showing clear evidence of bycatch, rising to over 51% when considering northern Portugal alone, suggesting local differences in porpoise occurrence and mortality hotspots. Between 2011 and 2015, an estimated annual average of 207 porpoises was removed due to bycatch in Portuguese waters, substantially exceeding the annual Potential Biological Removal (PBR) threshold of 22 porpoises (95% CI: 12–43) estimated for that period. Recent data from the northern Portuguese coast highlight a continued increase in harbour porpoise strandings with no evidence of a decline in bycatch rates. In 2023, 58 porpoises stranded in the northern coast of Portugal, the highest annual number ever documented for entire country. Estimated bycatch removals in 2022 and 2023 (107 and 187 individuals, respectively) resulted in annual population losses of 9.0–9.4%, significantly surpassing the Potential Biological Removal (PBR) thresholds of 10 and 17 individuals for the same years. The life history of the Iberian harbour porpoise revealed potential adaptive reproductive changes. Overall, female porpoises attained sexual maturity at 6.33 years and 166 cm total body length while males reach sexual maturity relatively earlier, at 4.98 years and with 149 cm. Comparing data from two different periods (period 1: 2000-2014; period 2: 2015-2023), males reached sexual maturity at smaller body lengths with reduced growth rates in the second period, likely to conserve energy for reproduction, while reinvesting in somatic growth later to enhance mobility and lifetime reproductive success. In contrast, females exhibit delayed sexual maturity, reduction in pregnancy rates (0.54 to 0.45) and longer calving intervals (1.85 to 2.22 years) in the second period, likely reflecting energy conservation strategies to ensure successful pregnancies and calf survival. These changes combined with the high pre-maturity female mortality suggest that the Iberian harbour porpoise population is facing great challenges to maintain population sustainability. The potential increase of porpoise densities in coastal hotspots due to the seasonal upwelling in spring/early summer (and increase in nearshore productivity) may enhance mating opportunities and fertilization success. Moreover, the seasonal strandings peak coinciding with the mating season and presence of dependent calves potentially reflects local higher densities, heightened activity and vulnerability to fisheries. Porpoise dietary data further underscore the overlap between fishing activities and porpoise feeding areas, resulting in high bycatch rates. Stomach contents analysis identified Trisopterus spp. and Chelon spp. together with Callionymus lyra (a non-commercial species) as the main prey of Iberian harbour porpoises in Portuguese waters. Isotopic concentrations confirmed coastal feeding habits in Iberian harbour porpoises, with muscle isotopes indicating pouting (Trisopterus luscus) as the primary prey. Temporal and seasonal dietary variations suggest that harbour porpoises replace predominant prey species according to availability, movements and/or seasonal energy requirements. Such shifts may reflect the influence of cumulative pressures, such as environmental changes and prey availability fluctuations. In Portugal, porpoise abundance estimates showed interannual fluctuations across the surveyed years, with abundance peaks in 2012–2013. Moreover, recent data revealed persistently low densities (0.048 ind/km² in 2022 and 0.079 ind/km² in 2023) along with a record increase in strandings (registered in 2023), suggesting that mortality patterns are not solely density dependent. The cyclic patterns of abundance estimates and strandings likely reflect ecological constraints in habitats where intense fishing pressure may also contribute to limiting their carrying capacity. Such environmental limitations may influence demographic parameters (such as reducing the number of mature females in recent years) and may drive adaptive responses that function as compensatory mechanisms. Despite these potential adaptive responses, recent estimates suggest that the population is failing to recover to the highest abundance estimates registered in 2012 and 2013 in Portuguese waters. Overall, the Iberian harbour porpoise population inhabits a critical habitat under severe anthropogenic pressures, primarily from fisheries, although cumulative effects from other current and emergent threats cannot be dismissed. Urgent crossborder conservation actions, including bycatch mitigation and habitat management, are needed to halt Iberian porpoise population.

records.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how foraging behavior and diet influence individual reproductive success is a key interest in evolutionary ecology. This is particularly true for capital breeding species where the accumulation and storage of energy to support offspring is critical, often following the “bigger‐is‐better” hypothesis. Using data collected from female gray seals ( Halichoerus grypus ) at Sable Island, Canada, between 1995 and 2018, we tested the hypothesis that differences in foraging effort and diet prior to the breeding season, estimated through satellite telemetry, stable isotope (SI) signatures, and quantitative fatty acid signature analysis (QFASA), respectively, affect reproductive success. There was no relationship between dominant prey type, the energy density of estimated diets, and maternal postpartum mass (MPPM). Females consuming a diet of lower diversity and with more positive δ 13 C estimates, possibly indicating more benthic foraging, had higher MPPM. MPPM was the best predictor of offspring mass at weaning. However, metrics of maternal foraging effort and diet alone did not influence pup weaning mass when MPPM was included in the model. These results suggest that different foraging strategies and diets can lead to sufficient body energy storage that enables reproductive success in a capital breeder. Considering this colony was increasing rapidly during the study period, the influence of foraging effort and diet might differ in a stable or declining population where intraspecific competition may be more evident.
records.title: Influence of Foraging Effort and Diet on Maternal Energy Stores and Offspring Weaning Mass in Gray Seals ( Halichoerus grypus )

records.abstract: Abstract Acoustic telemetry has become a widely used method to remotely monitor aquatic animal behaviour, and survival because of its relative affordability, miniature size, and extended battery life. However, its use in pinnipeds remains limited, partly due to ethical concerns of potential auditory disturbance, although limited scientific evidence exists on this aspect. Our study aims to address this knowledge gap by investigating whether animal-borne acoustic transmitters, using the common 69 kHz frequency, induce lethal or sub-lethal effects in seals, carrying the transmitter, during their most vulnerable life-stage: young-of-the-year. Between 2023 and 2025, we equipped a total of 130 weaned Atlantic grey seal pups ( Halichoerus grypus Fabricius, 1791) with satellite transmitters to monitor their behaviour and survival during their first year at sea. Approximately half—68 grey seals—were also fitted with a 69 kHz acoustic transmitter (producing a 3–5 s low power signal, source level 147 dB re 1 µPa @ 1 m in water, on average every 120 s). Compared to the control group, acoustically-tagged seals did not exhibit a higher haul out probability, associated with avoidance behaviour of acoustic signals that were only audible to them underwater. While at sea, acoustically-tagged seals allocated a higher proportion of time to widespread movement, compared to the control group, suggesting a prolonged exploration phase. However, this difference began diminishing by the third week at sea. Although the latter behavioural difference may support the presence of sub-lethal effects, overall survival did not differ between groups, during this sensitive life-stage. Collectively, these findings indicate that the effects of 69 kHz acoustic telemetry may be transient, acting primarily through early behavioural pathways; however, the underlying mechanism leading to the attenuation of the effect of the acoustic pings on seal behaviour remains unknown. The study suggests that animal-borne 69 kHz acoustic telemetry could be used as to study grey seal ecology over long time periods, while emphasizing that its use, like any telemetry method, requires weighing scientific benefits against potential consequences.
records.title: Potential effects of animal-borne 69 kHz acoustic telemetry on pinniped behaviour and survival in the wild

records.abstract: Marine ecosystems face multifaceted threats stemming from historical overexploitation and environmental degradation. Despite existing research, there are notable gaps in understanding the long-term dietary dynamics of marine organisms in the context of anthropogenic impacts. To address these gaps, we utilized stable isotope analysis as a proxy for dietary niche and examined changes in the Black Sea over a 4000-year period, focusing on ancient and contemporary samples from cetaceans ( Phocoena phocoena , Delphinus delphis , Tursiops truncatus ) and fish ( Scophthalmus maximus ). Among the ancient samples, the isotopic data from all four species revealed a wide and generally overlapping average dietary niche. In contrast, contemporary cetacean and fish samples exhibited niche compression, indicative of a fundamental shift in the Black Sea marine ecosystem from Antiquity to the present day. Our analyses provide ecologically significant temporal perspectives, shedding light on critical trends and changes essential for conservation efforts aimed at addressing contemporary ecological challenges in degraded marine systems.
records.journal: The Science of The Total Environment
records.title: A 4000-year record of parallel collapse in the ecological niche of Black Sea top predators

records.abstract: This study investigates cetacean occurrence and stranding records along the Romanian Black Sea coast between 2021 and 2025, focusing on the three resident subspecies: Tursiops truncatus ponticus, Delphinus delphis ponticus, and Phocoena phocoena relicta. A total of 1392 live individuals were documented across 188 sighting events, with T. t. ponticus and D. d. ponticus together representing 88.3% of all recorded individuals. The monthly distribution of recorded sighting events differed significantly among subspecies (p < 0.001), as did the distance of recorded sightings from the coastline (p < 0.001). Median distances were 4.40 km for T. t. ponticus, 61.78 km for D. d. ponticus, and 30.44 km for P. p. relicta. During the same period, 76 stranded cetaceans were recorded along the Romanian Black Sea coast, of which 58 were identified to subspecies level. P. p. relicta accounted for 70.7% of identified stranded individuals, compared with 11.7% of live individuals recorded during research cruises. Stranding records were most frequent in August and May, although their monthly distribution did not differ significantly among subspecies. Although both datasets covered the same geographical region and study period, differences in observation methods and sampling effort limit direct comparisons and prevent inferences about mortality rates or population trends. Nevertheless, the observed differences in the spatial and monthly distribution of live sightings, together with the high representation of P. p. relicta among stranded individuals, provide complementary information to support future cetacean monitoring, stranding investigations, and conservation efforts in the Romanian Black Sea.
records.title: Spatio-Temporal Distribution and Stranding Records of Cetaceans Along the Romanian Black Sea

records.abstract: In dieser Studie wurde ein RT-qPCR-basierter Arbeitsablauf zur Analyse der Expression der immunbezogenen Gene IL-6, IFN-γ, TLR2 und NF-κB im Blut von Kegelrobbenjungen etabliert und validiert. B2M und YWHAZ wurden als potenzielle Referenzgene evaluiert. Die Primerspezifität, die Amplifikationseffizienz sowie die quantitativen Messbereiche wurden mittels Schmelzkurvenanalyse, Agarose-Gel-Elektrophorese und anhand von Standardkurven, die aus in vitro transkribierter RNA erstellt wurden, bewertet. Die Genexpression wurde in Bezug auf Gesundheitszustand, Geschlecht, Ernährungsstadium, Schadstoffkonzentrationen und hämatologische Parameter analysiert. Alle Primerpaare lieferten spezifische Produkte, und die Standardkurven zeigten eine hohe Linearität. Die Analyse von IL-6 und IFN-γ war durch eine geringe Transkripthäufigkeit und Messwerte unterhalb der validierten Bestimmungsgrenze eingeschränkt. Die TLR2-Expression unterschied sich zwischen gesunden und erkrankten Robben, während keine Unterschiede zwischen Männchen und Weibchen festgestellt wurden. Bei IL-6, IFN-γ und NF-κB wurden Unterschiede zwischen Jungtieren und entwöhnten Jungtieren beobachtet. Da B2M und YWHAZ zwischen den Gruppen nach Gesundheitszustand und Ernährungsstadium nicht stabil waren, sind diese Ergebnisse mit Vorsicht zu interpretieren. Es wurden keine signifikanten Zusammenhänge zwischen der Expression der Zielgene und den Schadstoffkonzentrationen festgestellt, während explorative Korrelationen mit mehreren hämatologischen Parametern beobachtet wurden. Die qPCR- und Droplet-Digital-PCR-Messungen korrelierten stark für B2M, YWHAZ, TLR2 und NF-κB, obwohl sich ihre absoluten Kopienzahlen erheblich unterschieden Übersetzt mit DeepL.com (kostenlose Version)
